title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 16, 2026)
content: From AI startup RapidCanvas raising $29 million to BharatPe launching Agentic AI amid festive season, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors. Latest news BharatPe launches Agentic AI for businesses In the middle of the festive season, BharatPe Agentic AI brings an intelligent, 24x7 assistant to the BharatPe for Business app, built with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform on Google Cloud. The Agentic AI brings assistance, context and task execution together within the BharatPe for Business app. It can proactively follow up on requests, flag relevant issues and share updates, helping merchants spend less time navigating support processes and more time managing their businesses. With India’s festive demand already showing strong momentum, BharatPe Agentic AI brings an AI-first approach to supporting the merchants powering the country’s festive economy, helping them manage everyday business requirements with greater ease, responsiveness and personalisation. C-CAMP is selected as one of five research organisations with a funding of Rs 500 Cr by the Governemt Biotech research and innovation organisation, C-CAMP has been selected as one of five RDI Fund’s Focus Research Organisations or FROs with a declared funding allocation of Rs 500 crore by the Government of India towards investment in India’s deeptech innovation sector. C-CAMP will collaborate with its private partners and investors to build a total consortium funding of Rs1000 crore+ for supporting India’s most transformative deeptech life sciences startups that can create impact in India and beyond. As the only dedicated biotech organisation in the list, C-CAMP will aim to fund high-risk yet gamechanging biotech innovations that can redefine India’s healthcare, agriculture and environment. Bla Bli Blu turns EBITDA positive, achieves a Rs 250 crore annual run rate Gurugram-based fragrance startup Bla Bli Blu has turned EBITDA-positive. The company has achieved an annual run rate of Rs 250 crore, up from the Rs 100 crore it reported six months ago. Founded in 2025, Bla Bli Blu addresses a glaring gap in India’s fragrance market: shoppers’ options were limited to buying indistinguishable mass-market perfumes or paying a steep premium for international labels. Their quest for better consumer experience has manifested in Bla Bli Blu’s extensive, growing range of premium perfumes built around personalities and moods. Pharmaceutical and nutraceutical company Steadfast has invested over Rs 100cr in a new facility Pharmaceutical and nutraceutical company Steadfast Limited has invested over Rs 100 crore in establishing a fully integrated in-house Formulation Research & Development (FR&D) facility in Noida. The company states that with this investment in the facility, which commenced operations recently, it aims to contribute to building world-class research and nutraceutical manufacturing capabilities in India and strengthen the country’s self-reliance in nutraceutical manufacturing. The plant is capable of manufacturing supplements across different delivery formats, including tablets, powders, effervescent tablets, and capsules. It has an annual production capacity of 900 million tablets, 130 million capsules, 900 million effervescent tablets, and 6500 metric tonnes of powder. Funding news RapidCanvas raises $29M in Series B AI execution company RapidCanvas has raised $29 million in Series B funding led by Vertex Ventures SEA & India. The round also saw participation from Hitachi Ventures and existing investors, including Accel, Peak XV Partners, Valley Capital Partners and Titanium Ventures. The startup has raised a total funding to $52.5 million. RapidCanvas will use the Series B funding to grow its go-to-market teams and expand its network of private equity and advisory partners, who bring managed AI execution to their portfolio companies and clients. It will also grow its field AI engineering team across India, the U.S. and Brazil. Space robotics startup Cosmochute raises $1.5M Space robotics startup Cosmochute has raised $1.5 million in a pre-seed funding round led by Accel and Prosus Ventures, as part of the Atoms X program. IIMA Ventures’ Deep-tech and Aerospace Acceleration Fund, Operators Studio and Chinmayi Muthyala also participated in this round. The company is building robotics and infrastructure for the emerging lunar economy. Cosmochute joins six other startups from the inaugural Atoms X cohort launched earlier this year. The latest funding will enable Cosmochute to continue product development, strengthen its engineering team and advance its commercial roadmap as it works towards its next phase of growth. Banaraswala raises $2M in seed funding Banaraswala, Ghat se Ghar Tak, known for its Banarsi cuisine, has raised $2 million in seed funding from Prax Impex Private Limited. The money raised will help the brand enter new markets, innovate its menu and grow through franchises. Banaraswala is a company established by Vibhanshu Mishra and currently operates three outlets across Delhi and is in the process of expanding. The fresh capital will be deployed towards accelerating the brand’s pan-India expansion in QSR and banarasi molecular cuisine, strengthening its presence across emerging markets and significantly broadening its product portfolio over the coming months. (The copy will be updated with the latest news)

title: Magicbricks appoints Mayank Jain as CEO
content: Real estate classifieds Magicbricks has appointed Mayank Jain as chief executive officer (CEO), effective October 1. In a statement on Friday, Magicbricks, one of the leading property platforms, said Jain has joined from CarDekho, where he served for over five years as CEO of Auto Classifieds. Jain has more than two decades of experience across digital, media, technology and consumer businesses. "At Magicbricks, Mayank will focus on accelerating the company’s next phase of growth by leveraging its digital capabilities, advancing technology-led innovation and strengthening its consumer-centric approach," the company said. His priorities would include driving business transformation, improving operational and financial performance, and further reinforcing Magicbricks’ position in India’s evolving real estate ecosystem, it added. Jain holds an MBA from INSEAD, a PGDM from Management Development Institute (MDI), Gurgaon, and a degree in Computer Engineering. He will be based at Magicbricks’ Noida office and will report to N Subramanian, Executive Director and Group CEO of The Times Group. Magicbricks said it has monthly traffic exceeding 2 crores and an active base of over 15 lakh property listings. The company has become a full-stack service provider for all real estate needs, with services including home loans, interiors, and expert advice.

title: India’s AI opportunity could run into trillions of dollars, creating new possibilities for startups
content: India’s artificial intelligence (AI) opportunity could extend well beyond the $100 billion discussed by industry leaders, with the technology potentially adding $1 trillion to the country’s GDP by 2035. For startups, the opportunity lies in using AI to address large, underserved markets and building businesses that can scale across India and beyond. At a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project at Techsparks 2026 on the topic - India’s $100 Billion AI Opportunity, Ashutosh Sharma, Head of Investments and M&A, India, Prosus, and Keshav Reddy, Founder and CEO of Equal AI, highlighted how the technology could transform businesses, improve productivity and create new categories of consumer and enterprise companies. Ashutosh Sharma said previous technology waves, particularly the internet and smartphones, created large businesses by democratising access to products and services. AI could take this transformation further by democratising access to intelligence. “We are taking one more step. We are democratising something else, something new, and something much more powerful, and that’s intelligence. Everyone, after the proliferation of AI, will be more intelligent, more productive than before,” he said. He added that the internet and smartphone revolutions had already generated businesses worth billions of dollars by helping consumers meet previously unmet needs. “There is no doubt in my mind. With something that is more powerful, the outcomes will only be larger. $100 billion, trillion? I don’t know,” he said, pointing to the potentially enormous scale of the AI opportunity. For Indian startups, Ashutosh Sharma believes the opportunity exists across virtually every sector. India has a large consumer market, a substantial talent pool and access to venture capital and private equity funding. More importantly, the country has numerous problems that could be addressed using AI. He identified the shortage of quality education as one example of an area where AI-powered products could bridge the gap between demand and supply. Healthcare and other essential services offer similar opportunities for entrepreneurs to develop scalable solutions. Reddy said India’s large-scale adoption of AI presents an opportunity for domestic companies to capture more of the value generated by the technology. “We are the largest consuming AI country in the world, and it is only going to get more and more and more, and we need to make sure that that value is captured by Indian companies, by Indian consumers,” he said. Reddy cited Equal AI’s experience as an example of how addressing a specific consumer problem can create opportunities for rapid growth. The company developed an AI-native call assistant in response to the prevalence of spam calls in India, where phone calls and messages remain important modes of communication. According to figures shared during the discussion, Equal AI grew from around 70,000 monthly active users in January to 3.5 million in the preceding month. It was forecasting 15 million monthly active users by March. The company had also crossed one million daily active users and was targeting 10 million daily active users over the following 12 months. “You have to go deep, find a problem, solve it well, and then just expand from there,” Reddy said, explaining the approach that startups could adopt to build successful AI businesses. He also stressed the need for Indian companies to build consumer technology platforms capable of competing with global players. However, he identified computing costs as a major constraint on AI businesses seeking to serve millions of users. Ashutosh Sharma said local understanding would be a key differentiator for Indian startups competing with international companies. Businesses that understand the nuances of Indian consumers and their everyday challenges could develop products better suited to the domestic market. The panellists also urged entrepreneurs to focus on building sustainable competitive advantages. Sharma said falling product development costs and faster innovation cycles made it essential for founders to identify what would protect their businesses over the long term. “The market is not a moat anymore,” he said, urging founders to think from the outset about the competitive advantage they were building. Reddy emphasised the need for patient capital and a long-term commitment to entrepreneurship, noting that building large technology businesses often involves years of experimentation and failure. For India's startup ecosystem, the opportunity is therefore not limited to the size of the AI market itself. The larger prize lies in converting the country's consumer scale, technology talent and unmet demand into globally competitive AI products and platforms. Whether the opportunity ultimately reaches $100 billion or extends into trillions of dollars will depend on how effectively Indian businesses deploy AI to solve real-world problems and capture the resulting economic value.

title: Snabbit FY26 loss widens multifold to Rs 167.75 Cr; revenue rises to Rs 12.25 Cr
content: Maestroedge Solutions, which runs home services platform Snabbit, has posted a net loss of Rs 167.75 crore for 2025-26, nearly 30 times lower than the previous year, as spending on service providers, marketing and staff rose with the expansion of its business, according to financial statements filed with the Registrar of Companies. The Mumbai-based company reported a loss of Rs 5.70 crore in FY25. Its revenue from operations rose to Rs 12.25 crore in FY26 from Rs 26.35 lakh a year earlier. Platform services brought in Rs 10.82 crore, and the sale of uniforms to its service providers, whom it calls experts, stood at Rs 1.42 crore. Other income was Rs 14.77 crore, while total income was recorded at Rs 27 crore. Total expenses rose to Rs 194.76 crore from Rs 6.81 crore in FY25. Expert service cost was the largest expense at Rs 63.07 crore, up from Rs 27 lakh. Marketing spending rose nearly 60-fold to Rs 48.69 crore. Employee benefit expenses grew to Rs 46.02 crore from Rs 3.27 crore, and service fulfilment expenses to Rs 23.83 crore from Rs 48 lakh. "FY26 was our first full year of operations, and we made a deliberate choice to invest ahead of scale to build a category, not just a company," Snabbit founder and CEO Aayush Agarwal said. Agarwal said the company began the year with about 500 jobs a day across eight micro-markets and ended it at a run rate of 35,000 daily jobs across more than 100 micro-markets. During the year, it acquired nearly a million customers and onboarded over 20,000 experts, according to Agarwal. Losses were mainly due to investments in geographic expansion, customer and expert acquisition, and long-term operating capabilities, Agarwal added. The company was incorporated in January 2024. Its platform lets customers book house help, with an initial focus on maids for cleaning and cooking. The company had 309 employees as of March 31, 2026. Agarwal, who holds 98.98% of its equity shares, drew a salary of Rs 60 lakh in FY26, up from Rs 15.47 lakh. "Given the pace of growth and the investments required to build this category from the ground up, FY26 financials do not fully reflect the underlying economics or the maturity of the business today. "As we continue to scale, the benefits of operating leverage, improving unit economics and increasing network density are becoming increasingly evident," Agarwal said.

title: AI execution company RapidCanvas raises $29M in Series B
content: AI execution company RapidCanvas has raised $29 million in Series B funding led by Vertex Ventures SEA & India. The round also saw participation from Hitachi Ventures and existing investors, including Accel, Peak XV Partners, Valley Capital Partners and Titanium Ventures. The startup has raised a total funding to $52.5 million. RapidCanvas will use the Series B funding to grow its go-to-market teams and expand its network of private equity and advisory partners, who bring managed AI execution to their portfolio companies and clients. It will also grow its field AI engineering team across India, the US and Brazil. Further, the company plans to invest in its three products: deepening the Enterprise Context Engine, expanding the skills library behind the Visual Development Canvas, and strengthening governance in the Operational Harness. RapidCanvas pairs its AI platform with field AI engineers to deliver custom AI solutions. AI engineers learn each customer's business processes, design and build custom AI applications, and stay accountable for the applications' outcomes after delivery. The RapidCanvas AI platform brings together three products: The Enterprise Context Engine lets an enterprise capture how a business process runs, from requirements and tribal knowledge to data schemas and decision history, and the enterprise owns that context. The Visual Development Canvas lets AI engineers rapidly build custom AI solutions that meet industry benchmarks, drawing on a skills library that gives each new solution a 60% head start from proven, benchmarked code. The Operational Harness manages and governs AI solutions once they're deployed in production. RapidCanvas offers its Hybrid Approach at subscription pricing, changing the economics of enterprise AI. So far in 2026, more than 75 enterprises in manufacturing, financial services, retail, business services and infrastructure have made 1.4 million AI-led decisions with applications built on RapidCanvas. More than 40% of RapidCanvas' customers now run multiple AI use cases in production, said the company in a press statement. "AI can be the great equaliser, but so far its biggest wins have gone to the Fortune 100. We want to give every enterprise the same opportunity," said Rahul Pangam, co-founder and CEO of RapidCanvas. "Vibe coding has made it easy to start building with AI. Getting AI into production reliably and safely still remains the biggest gap. Our growth over the past six quarters is evidence that AI in enterprises is moving beyond pilots into production and real operations." RapidCanvas serves an underserved market: enterprises with $100 million to $10 billion in revenue that have AI budgets and C-suite mandates but no proven path to outcomes. In conversations with more than 400 business leaders, RapidCanvas found that most C-level executives expect a return on AI within six to 12 months, yet very few have moved beyond pilots and proofs of concept.

title: India can build anything: Prof. Ashok Jhunjhunwala; Food Pharmer’s shift to food startup founder
content: Hello, While Swiggy’s existing users continue to order, the real expansion lies in tapping into the nearly 90% of Indians who have never used food delivery. Speaking at YourStory’s TechSparks 2026, Rohit Kapoor, CEO of Swiggy's Food Marketplace, highlighted that driving future growth hinges on attracting these new consumers. Peak XV Managing Director Mohit Bhatnagar said the success of companies such as Zomato and the growing acceptance of startups in India's public markets have fundamentally changed what founders and investors believe is possible. Indian startup founders are increasingly aspiring to build companies worth $50 billion or even $100 billion, a shift that is prompting venture capital firms such as Peak XV Partners to take bigger risks, according to Bhatnagar. Meanwhile, India’s primary challenge in educating 247 million students is structural rather than numerical, as traditional schooling remains stuck in nineteenth-century methods despite society entering the intelligence era. Speaking at TechSparks 2026, leaders from Sri Chaitanya Group and Intel highlighted the need to end the legacy practice of treating technology as an isolated subject. Instead, education must integrate technical tools directly into daily learning to reflect modern workplaces where technology and work are seamlessly merged. Lastly, IT services company Wipro on Thursday reported a slight decline of 1.40% in consolidated net profit to Rs 3,200.6 crore for the July-September quarter of FY27. The Bengaluru-headquartered company had posted a net profit (attributable to owners of the company) of Rs 3,246.2 crore in the year-ago period, Wipro said in a regulatory filing. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about India can build anything: Prof. Ashok Jhunjhunwala Food Pharmer’s shift to food startup founder Here’s your trivia for today: Before moving into high-end acoustics, what German manufacturer made vacuum tubes and microphones under the original name “Laboratorium Wennebostel”? TechSparks India can build anything: Prof. Ashok Jhunjhunwala Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Padma Shri Prof. Ashok Jhunjhunwala emphasised that while India possesses world-class engineering talent, a heavy reliance on importing physical products persists because technical education prioritizes theory over hands-on building. To achieve complete technological self-reliance, he urges backing risk-taking young entrepreneurs, particularly from Tier II, III, and IV cities, and overhauling overburdened university curricula to foster practical creation and lifelong learning. Key takeaways: Indian engineers can build virtually any technology, yet the country still imports almost all of its physical products. Curricula should cut half of their theoretical coursework to make space for practical building, peer learning, and continuous self-education. While established industries remain risk-averse, young founders—especially in smaller cities—are the primary drivers of national tech self-reliance. TechSparks Food Pharmer’s shift to food startup founder Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Revant Himatsingka, popularly known as Food Pharmer, outlined his transition from an uncompromising health activist to the founder of Only What’s Needed (OWN). Facing extreme legal and commercial backlash for exposing misleading claims by major FMCG brands, Himatsingka launched OWN to provide truly transparent food alternatives. Clean food: Transitioning from critic to creator means operating under zero margin for error; any mistake in product safety or labeling will be magnified instantly due to his public profile. OWN replaces vague ingredient lists with precise pie charts on the front of packaging and offers QR codes in major Indian languages so consumers can easily see exact percentages without reading hidden fine print. Himatsingka deliberately rejects traditional marketing strategies—avoiding "green-washed" packaging, omitting his own face from the box, running no discount promotions, and relying on open supply-chain disclosures rather than ad spend. News & updates Profits: Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion as it prepares for its IPO reportedly planned for November, CNBC reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Telecom: Jio Platforms plans to raise revenue per customer mainly by selling more services rather than lifting tariffs, though it keeps the option of higher prices, Managing Director Akash Ambani said on Thursday, days before the Reliance Industries unit opens what would be India's largest initial public offering. title: Welcome competition but Indian laws apply to all: Reliance breaks silence on Musk's satcom row
content: Reliance Industries Ltd on Friday broke its silence on Elon Musk's public criticism of India's satellite communications landscape, saying it sees a competitive market as the true test of who serves customers best, and welcomes competition, including from Starlink, but asserted that every player must obey Indian laws. In its first direct response to Musk's recent barbs, the company said it was placing "the facts on record." Musk had criticised Reliance and argued that more competition would benefit consumers in satcom. "At Reliance, we have never feared competition. We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best," the Mukesh Ambani--led company said in a statement. The company backed its stance citing Jio's own record. Jio entered India's crowded telecom market in 2016 as the newest player, with not a single customer, and in a matter of just ten years, earned the trust of over 530 million customers, offering Indians some of the best digital infrastructure and most affordable data in the world, it said. "We welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink. Every player, Jio included, must serve the people of India and abide by the laws and policies of the land," the statement said. Reliance said India's openness to investment and innovation, homegrown or international, rests on the rule of law. "Like every Indian enterprise, Reliance has grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international, that improve the lives of the people. That openness rests on the rule of law," it said. As the government has maintained, it applies the same process to every applicant, Indian or foreign, Reliance said, adding "Jio's own satellite services await clearances". Earlier this week, addressing the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, Bharti Airtel Chairman Sunil Mittal said his satellite communications venture Eutelsat OneWeb was significantly ahead of Elon Musk's Starlink in the queue to launch services in India. His remarks added a fresh twist to a public dispute over regulatory approvals and competition in the country's satellite internet market. Government sources, responding to the controversy surrounding Starlink and Musk's recent claims, have made it clear that any company operating in India must comply with the law of the land. The Centre's position has been clear and consistent throughout, they added. "Government's position has been very clear, and was so even at the time they had applied, that if you don't follow Indian laws, you cannot do business here...So to do business here, you have to follow Indian laws," sources had said.. "I think I am significantly ahead in the queue from him. I applied five years back," Mittal said, and added "We don't have the permission, so we'll be very happy to get it at least a few days before him". Mittal said OneWeb's ground network has been ready for three years, and its satellites have been hovering over India for five years, but the company is still awaiting permission to begin commercial operations. The pushback from Mittal, and now Reliance, comes after Musk, the world's richest man, accused powerful business interests of blocking Starlink's entry into India. In a series of posts on social media platform X recently, Musk took aim at Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani, sarcastically addressing him as "Prime Minister Ambani" and questioning whether he wielded greater influence over India's decisions than Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Musk has alleged that some business groups are seeking to preserve a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers. However, the Ministry of Communications rejected the charge, describing suggestions that the regulatory framework or its application was unfair or discriminatory as "baseless and misconceived". The government said satellite operators must meet the same regulatory requirements, including security conditions and spectrum allocation rules, before they can begin commercial services. Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said three ventures -- Musk's Starlink, Reliance's Jio Satcom and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb -- had secured satellite communications licences. Amazon's Project Kuiper has expressed interest but must follow the established procedure, he said. Scindia made it clear that spectrum would be assigned once the government finalised a revenue-based charging framework and individual operators fulfilled security requirements. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) and the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) were close to a decision on satellite spectrum pricing, he added. The distinction between a licence and operational approval is central to the dispute: securing a licence does not automatically allow a company to begin commercial services. Spectrum assignment and the fulfilment of security conditions remain key steps. The dispute comes at a consequential time for Reliance, which is preparing for the initial public offering of Jio Platforms, its digital services business. Jio has set a price band of Rs 1,065 to 1,119 a share for its offer of up to 27 crore new shares, about 3 per cent of the existing capital, with no offer-for-sale component. At the top of the band, the sale would raise about Rs 30,213 crore, ahead of Hyundai Motor India's Rs 27,870 crore share sale in October 2024, the country's biggest. The price implies a market value of about Rs 10.3 lakh crore, short of the roughly Rs 11 lakh crore the company had earlier been said to seek. Bidding runs from October 21 to 23, with anchor investors bidding on October 19. The shares are expected to begin trading on October 28. Reliance is also developing its satellite ambitions, including a proposed constellation of about 1,600 low-earth-orbit satellites aimed at extending internet connectivity to 600,000 villages. That would put Jio in more direct competition with Starlink, which is seeking access to a vast market where satellite broadband could serve remote communities and locations poorly covered by terrestrial networks. Ironically, Reliance and SpaceX last year signed an agreement to explore ways of bringing Starlink services to Indian customers through Jio's retail network.

title: Shubhra Saxena’s It Matters A Lot: 5 Lessons on conscious living
content: I attended the launch of It Matters A Lot by author and bureaucrat Shubhra Saxena on October 16, 2026, at the India Habitat Centre in New Delhi. Published by Rupa Publications, the book features a foreword by the Dalai Lama and explores self-awareness, conscious choices and what makes life meaningful. The event brought together personalities from literature, diplomacy, academia, healthcare and public service, including Gurcharan Das, Pavan K. Verma, Prof. Kusum Lata Kedia, Abha Sharma and Dr Shweta Mathur Lall. The discussions reflected the book’s call to pause and reconsider our beliefs, relationships and ambitions. At a time when success is often measured through professional achievements and social recognition, It Matters A Lot asks whether we are living by our own values or following others’ expectations. Spanning life stages from childhood to old age, the book examines how upbringing, relationships, social conditioning and life experiences shape our perspectives. Rather than offering a formula for happiness, Saxena encourages readers to question their assumptions and discover what gives their lives meaning. Here are five important lessons from It Matters A Lot that encourage readers to reflect on their lives and embrace conscious living. 5 Lessons from It Matters A Lot by Shubhra Saxena 1. Question what success means to you Success is often defined by society through career progression, financial security, recognition and status. While these achievements can be meaningful, they do not necessarily guarantee contentment. It Matters A Lot encourages readers to examine whether their ambitions reflect their genuine desires or the expectations of family, peers and society. The pursuit of conventional milestones can become automatic when we rarely question why we want them in the first place. The lesson is to develop a personal understanding of success. Instead of measuring your life entirely against someone else's achievements, consider what gives you a sense of purpose, fulfilment and peace. 2. Understand how your past shapes you Our understanding of ourselves begins forming long before we can consciously evaluate our beliefs. Childhood experiences, family relationships, parental expectations and social norms influence how we approach relationships, handle challenges and perceive our own worth. These influences can remain with us well into adulthood, sometimes shaping our decisions without our awareness. Saxena's exploration of life's different stages invites readers to look back at these formative experiences and consider their continuing influence. Recognising the origins of our beliefs does not mean blaming our past. It means understanding which patterns serve us and which may need to change. Self-awareness begins when we learn to distinguish between what we have inherited and what we consciously choose to believe. 3. Make choices instead of following expectations From education and careers to relationships and family responsibilities, life presents countless decisions shaped by social expectations. It can be difficult to distinguish our own preferences from the pressure to meet other people's standards. The book encourages readers to question whether their choices reflect their values or a desire for acceptance and approval. Living consciously does not mean rejecting every expectation or disregarding the people around us. It means understanding why we make particular decisions and taking responsibility for their consequences. Before committing to a goal or making an important decision, ask yourself whether it aligns with the life you want to build. Even small moments of reflection can help you approach life with greater independence and intention. 4. Treat relationships with greater empathy Self-understanding is not limited to personal growth. It can also transform the way we relate to other people. When we become more aware of our own insecurities, emotional responses and assumptions, we may find it easier to recognise that other people have their own struggles, experiences and perspectives. This awareness can reduce unnecessary conflict and encourage more thoughtful communication. It Matters A Lot connects conscious living with empathy, compassion and responsibility towards others. Its broader message is that a meaningful life is not measured solely by individual accomplishments but also by the quality of our relationships and the care we extend to the people around us. Understanding ourselves can become a starting point for understanding others. 5. Accept change and rethink what matters Life rarely unfolds exactly as planned. Ambitions change, relationships evolve, opportunities disappear, and loss becomes part of the human experience. As people move through adulthood, midlife and old age, their priorities may change alongside their circumstances. The book encourages readers to reflect on these transitions rather than remain attached to outdated definitions of success or happiness. Acceptance does not mean giving up on personal growth. It means recognising that some circumstances cannot be controlled and learning to respond to them with greater clarity. As life changes, the things that once seemed essential may become less important, while relationships, inner peace, compassion and a sense of meaning may take on greater significance. Conscious living requires us to keep asking what matters to us now, rather than assuming that yesterday's priorities must define tomorrow. Why it matters a lot is relevant today Modern life leaves little room for reflection, with work, digital distractions and the pressure to achieve more often taking priority over questions of meaning and fulfilment. Saxena’s book encourages readers to examine their habits, assumptions and priorities. Rather than offering quick fixes, it uses questions at the end of each chapter to help readers find insights that reflect their own experiences and values. The book also connects self-awareness with empathy and responsibility towards others, showing how personal reflection can shape our relationships, communities and the way we live. Final thoughts In It Matters A Lot , Shubhra Saxena explores questions of identity, ambition, beliefs and what makes life meaningful. Featuring a foreword by His Holiness the Dalai Lama and published by Rupa Publications, the book encourages readers to reflect on their choices, cultivate self-awareness and practise compassion through different stages of life. At its heart, the book reminds us that living well means looking beyond milestones to understand our purpose, value our relationships and focus on what truly matters.

title: 7 Books that explain why we're connected but still lonely
content: You can have hundreds of followers, dozens of unread messages and conversations happening across multiple apps, yet still feel as though you have no one to talk to when life gets difficult. You can spend hours scrolling through other people's lives and still feel disconnected from your own. In a world where reaching someone takes seconds, loneliness has become a surprisingly familiar experience. Technology has changed how we maintain friendships, meet new people and share our experiences. Yet constant communication does not always translate into emotional closeness. A like cannot always replace a meaningful conversation, and a video call cannot always provide the comfort of being physically present with someone. Understanding this contradiction requires looking beyond screen time and social media habits. Loneliness is also connected to how we build relationships, experience belonging and find meaning in our communities. These seven books explore why modern life can leave us feeling disconnected, even when we are more digitally connected than ever. 1. Alone Together by Sherry Turkle In Alone Together , sociologist Sherry Turkle explores how technology changes our relationships and our expectations of companionship. We can communicate constantly through messages and social media while avoiding the deeper conversations that help us understand one another. The book asks an important question: are our digital connections making our relationships more meaningful, or simply making us feel less alone for a moment? 2. The Lonely Century by Noreena Hertz Noreena Hertz examines how technology, changing workplaces and weakening community ties contribute to isolation. The Lonely Century argues that loneliness is not simply an individual problem; it is also shaped by the way modern societies are organised. The book encourages readers to consider how stronger communities, meaningful interactions and shared experiences can help rebuild a sense of belonging. 3. Digital Minimalism by Cal Newport Checking notifications can make us feel socially active without necessarily helping us build closer relationships. In Digital Minimalism , Cal Newport explores how constant digital engagement can distract us from activities that bring genuine satisfaction. He encourages readers to use technology more intentionally and prioritise valuable experiences, including hobbies, focused conversations and spending time with people in person. 4. The Anxious Generation by Jonathan Haidt Jonathan Haidt examines the relationship between smartphone-based childhoods, social media and young people's mental well-being. The Anxious Generation explores how increased online engagement and reduced opportunities for independent play and face-to-face interaction may affect young people's development. It offers a starting point for understanding why digital connection does not always provide the emotional benefits of real-world friendships. Also Read 7 Books that explore the complexity of human relationships 5. Bowling Alone by Robert D. Putnam In Bowling Alone , political scientist Robert D. Putnam examines the decline of community participation and social connections in American life. He explores how people have become less involved in certain shared activities and organisations, weakening the relationships that help communities function. Although the book focuses primarily on the United States, its ideas offer a useful perspective on why belonging requires more than having a large online network. 6. Together by Vivek H. Murthy In Together , physician Vivek H. Murthy explores loneliness as a social and public health concern. He explains why human connection matters and how relationships, community involvement and everyday acts of care can help people feel less isolated. The book reminds readers that meaningful connection does not always require a large social circle; even a few supportive relationships can make a difference. 7. Reclaiming Conversation by Sherry Turkle Sherry Turkle returns to the relationship between technology and human connection in Reclaiming Conversation . She explores how the convenience of texting and online communication can sometimes come at the expense of meaningful conversation . By examining relationships at home, work and school, Turkle makes the case for giving people our full attention and creating space for conversations that build empathy and trust. Final thoughts Being connected is not the same as feeling connected. Social media helps us stay in touch, but meaningful relationships need trust, understanding and emotional closeness. These seven books explore modern loneliness, the role of technology and the importance of community. They encourage us to use digital spaces more mindfully and invest in real connections. Sometimes, feeling less lonely means spending less time seeking connections and more time nurturing the ones that matter.

title: Tech can improve governance, says Krishna Byre Gowda; Why Indian startups should build for the world from day one
content: Dear Reader, TechSparks 2026 continued to enthral and inspire. Day 2 of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup summit saw key conversations around deeptech, venture capital, and technology in governance. Krishna Byre Gowda, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Government of Karnataka, highlighted technology’s role in improving governance, enhancing transparency, and reducing corruption. He also said technology can help bridge the trust gap between people and the government. Highlighting Bengaluru’s economic weight in GCC investments and IT service exports, he urged entrepreneurs and builders to apply their innovation beyond commercial software to real socio-economic challenges. “ Bengaluru continues to be the centre for dynamism that nurtures talent and is able to be the home for a lot of people who contribute productively to their own lives, the economy, and the services of the country as well as the larger global space,” said Gowda. In a panel discussion on deeptech capital , venture capitalists said the deeptech ecosystem is giving rise to new kinds of founders and bold ideas. VCs focused on the deeptech segment believe Indian founders have several differentiated capabilities that can lead to the creation of self-reliant technologies. The panellists emphasised that deeptech founders must identify niche areas and build solutions around them, as the traditional manner of creating products will no longer work. In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, Tally’s Managing Director Tejas Goenka and Executive Director Nupur Goenka spoke about how the company has stayed relevant for 40 years. Here’s what’s in store for Day 3 , the final day of TechSparks 2026. In today’s newsletter, we will talk about Why Indian startups should build for the world from day one Govern like a bank, build like Big Tech: PhonePe’s Sameer Nigam Here’s your trivia for today: What is the name of the Japanese optical giant, founded in 1919 as Takachiho Seisakusho, famous for pioneering medical endoscopes and cameras? (Scroll down for the answer) TechSparks Why Indian startups should build for the world from day one Indian startups no longer need to wait until they establish themselves at home to expand internationally. Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director of Stripe India, says founders can think global and build for international markets from day one. At TechSparks 2026, he highlighted the role of payments infrastructure, localisation and AI in helping Indian businesses scale across borders. Key takeaways AI is making it faster and cheaper for Indian founders to build businesses for international markets, without waiting to establish a strong domestic presence. Stripe data shows 76% of customers prefer paying in their own currency, while offering local payment methods beyond cards can increase revenue by around 12%. As AI adoption increases spending on tokens and computing, Stripe’s planned OpenRouter acquisition aims to help businesses manage AI costs while building sustainable business models. Nigam also spoke about taking UPI to feature phones and making financial services accessible to more Indians.
